title: Direction
does: `direction down` makes the main flow run top to bottom instead of left to right.
effect: Layered things (tiers behind firewalls, a request path through zones) fit a page better going down; pipelines and lifecycles read better going right.
syntax: direction down
use: Tiers or layers that traffic crosses in order (a network behind firewalls): down. Pipelines and lifecycles: right, the default.

title: Title, caption and title block
does: `title` is drawn above the diagram, `caption` adds a muted line under it, and `title-block { key: value }` a small table at the bottom right: author, date, version, anything.
effect: The drawing moves down to make room for the title and caption, and grows at the bottom for the title block. A long caption wraps to the drawing's width. Nothing else moves.
use: For any diagram that leaves your hands: the title says what it is, the title block who made it and when.

title: Node kinds
does: A kind in square brackets says what a node is: `store`, `engine`, `pill`, `ask`, `start`, `final`, `state`.
effect: Kinds change the shape and colour, not the place. The layout only needs them for size: a pill is a little wider than a box.
syntax:
store db: Orders DB
ask ok: In stock?
pill u: Customer
use: To say what a node is: a person or outside actor, a data store, a decision, a state.

title: Icons
does: Any Lucide icon name in the brackets, or one of the common names (`database`, `firewall`, `user`...). `top` puts the icon above the text.
effect: Icons are drawn left of the text, so a node gets a little wider; with `top` it gets taller instead. Nothing else moves.
syntax:
fw [firewall]: Edge firewall
lb [loadbalancer top]: Load balancer
use: For recognisable things (database, firewall, user, cloud). Not on decisions or states. Any Lucide icon name works.

title: Technology logos
does: A technology’s name in the brackets draws its logo: small, before the technology’s name under the node’s own name when the node has a role icon; in the icon’s place when it has none; before the title of a zone.
effect: You see what each part does (the role icon) and what it is built with (the logo and its name). The note starts with the technology’s name (“Redis · sessions, 1 h”); with no role icon, the logo takes the icon’s place. Logos are in one colour.
use: Use it when the technologies matter to the reader (an architecture review, a migration). Any Simple Icons name; short names for common ones (kafka, postgres, k8s, node).

title: Link styles
does: Labels after a colon; `-->` dashed, `<->` both ways, `--` no arrowhead; tags `ok`, `bad`, `muted`, `dashed`.
effect: Labels take room in the layout (they sit beside the link and push things apart). The style of a link never changes where things go.
syntax:
a -> b : 443/tcp
a --> b          # dashed
a <-> b          # both ways
a -> b [bad]     # red
use: On every network link: ports and protocols cost nothing and make the diagram worth reading.

title: Where a link label goes
does: `[label-start]` or `[label-end]` puts a link's label just past its source or just before its target; `[label-above]`, `[label-below]`, `[label-left]`, `[label-right]` choose the side. A label in three parts, `start | middle | end`, also names the two ends.
effect: The ports sit next to the firewall that enforces them, “yes” next to the question, and each uplink names the interface at both ends. A hint is a preference: when its place is taken the label goes where there is room, and the result says so.
beforeLabel: Labels where the engine puts them
afterLabel: With position tags and end labels
syntax:
fw -> app : 443/tcp [label-end]
ask -> fix : no [label-start below]
core -> sw : ge-0/0/1 | uplink | port 24
core -> sw : ge-0/0/1 | | port 24     # ends only
use: When a label belongs to one end of a link: a port at the device that opens it, an interface name, a decision's yes and no. A label that needs a | of its own goes in quotes.

title: Frames
does: A frame draws a titled zone around its members; colours are `green`, `blue`, `orange`, `purple`, `grey`.
effect: Members of a frame are kept together, and the frame is drawn tight around them after the layout. Links that leave a zone cross its border.
use: For zones, networks, teams, anything that belongs together. Put the address range or owner in the title.

title: Nested frames
does: Frames nest: a zone inside a zone.
effect: Each frame is laid out on its own and then placed in its parent, so an inner zone stays together even when links pull its members apart.
use: For a zone inside a zone: a cluster in a region, a subnet in a VPC.

title: Column and row
does: `column` stacks nodes top to bottom, `row` side by side, inside the layout.
effect: Members of a stack get the same width and line up like a table. Links between members run straight.
use: For peers that one node feeds or that feed one node. They share a width and link in straight lines.

title: Siblings across the flow
does: In a `direction down` diagram, put siblings in a `row`; in a `direction right` one, in a `column`.
effect: Stacked along the flow, nodes stand in each other's way: the link to the one behind leaves sideways, runs round and comes back. Across the flow every node has a clear line.
use: Whenever several nodes sit next to a zone's entry point: across the flow (a row when the diagram goes down, a column when it goes right).

title: Rows and columns of frames
does: A `row` or `column` that holds frames places them side by side or one above the other, in the order written, and draws nothing itself.
effect: You decide who is next to whom: a grid of zones instead of a chain. Links still decide the details inside each zone.
use: When you want two zones next to each other, or a particular order. Do not wrap zones that the flow already stacks: it adds nothing.

title: Side zone
does: A frame tagged `side` stands beside the main flow instead of after it: to the right of a diagram that flows down, below one that flows right. `left` and `top` choose the other side.
effect: Without the tag the zone is the next tier, stacked under the data zone like any other. With it the rest of the diagram goes in a block of its own, the zone in a block beside it, and the zone sits level with the zones it is linked to. Links must go between nodes (a collector, a gateway), not to the zone itself.
use: For what watches or administers the diagram rather than being part of its path: logs, metrics, admin access.

title: Side zone that spans
does: `[side span]` makes a side zone as tall as the zones it is linked to (as wide, beside a flow to the right): from the top of the first to the bottom of the last.
effect: The nodes inside move level with what they are linked to, so the links across the gutter are straight. A zone without `span` keeps its own height, and spanning zones on the same side make room for it.
use: When the zone talks to several tiers and the links should run straight across.

title: Side zones on both sides
does: A diagram has two sides across its flow, so one side zone can go on each: admin access on the left, observability on the right.
effect: Each is placed level with the zones it is linked to. More than one on a side stack along it (next example).
syntax:
frame admin "admin access" [side left span] { ... }
frame obs "observability" [side span] { ... }
use: One zone on each side keeps both close to what they talk to.

title: Two side zones on one side
does: Two or more side zones on the same side stack along it, in the order of where their links come from.
effect: With `span` each takes its own slice of the length: where the ranges they are linked to overlap, the line between them is halfway. A zone without `span` keeps its place and the others make room. More than two on a side is a sign to split the diagram.
syntax:
frame obs "observability" [side span] { ... }
frame sec "security" [side span] { ... }
use: For two cross-cutting zones on the same side.

title: Span node
does: `span` makes a node as wide (or tall) as the stack it links to.
effect: Two sources feeding one node are further apart than the node is wide, so their links slide inward and bunch up. A span node has one attachment point under each source: both links drop straight.
syntax: ddos [span shield]: DDoS scrubbing
use: When two or more sources feed one node and their links bunch up at its edge.

title: Bridge node
does: `bridge` puts a node on the border between two zones.
effect: A firewall or gateway that belongs to two zones is drawn half in each, and the two zones are made to touch. Without it the firewall floats inside one of them.
syntax: fw [bridge span firewall]: Internal firewall
use: For a firewall or gateway that sits on the border of two zones.

title: Same width, same height
does: `same-width a b c` makes frames (or nodes) as wide as the widest; `same-height` likewise.
effect: A statement about relations, not a number: it keeps working when a label changes. The frames share their edges, so a stack of tiers has straight sides.
syntax: same-width edge core access
use: When the tiers of a diagram have ragged sides. Also `same-height`.

title: Align
does: `align slo rollback` puts nodes in different blocks on one line across the flow (here the rollback, outside the production zone, under the decision that leads to it).
effect: The blocks and zones are slid into line on those nodes, so the link between them is straight. A node in a zone moves with its whole zone. The engine already levels most linked pairs on its own; `align` is for the ones it does not, such as a node centred in a column of wider blocks.
syntax: align slo rollback
use: When a link between two blocks keeps a step the engine does not take out, or to choose which pair is level. It does not remove crossings.

title: Rail
does: A `rail` is a band along one edge for links that touch many nodes: logs, metrics, schedules.
effect: Rail links leave the layout entirely: each runs straight to a bus on the edge. The diagram looks as it did before the links were added.
use: For links that touch many nodes and are not part of the story: logs, metrics, schedulers.

title: Reversed link
does: `pg <- worker` draws the arrow into `pg` but places the worker after it.
effect: Both are laid out the same, with the worker on the far side. Only the arrow changes: it points at the node that is acted on. Use it when the story reads one way and the arrow the other (a worker polls the database: the worker comes later, the arrow goes to the database).
beforeLabel: pg -> worker (the arrow points at the worker)
afterLabel: pg <- worker (the arrow points into pg)
syntax: pg <- worker : claim a job
use: When the arrow should point one way and the story reads the other.

title: Legend
does: `key` lines add a legend under the diagram.
effect: The legend takes no part in the layout. It is laid out in a row below everything.
syntax:
key box [dashed] : retired
key -> [bad] : failure path
use: When colours, dashes or shapes carry meaning the reader has to learn.

title: Mark
does: The links into one node are not drawn. Each node they come from carries that node’s icon after its name instead, in the colour of its zone, and the legend says what the icon means.
effect: A node that most of the diagram uses (feature flags, a config service, an identity provider) no longer pulls a fan of links across every tier. The links stay in the source: delete the line and they are drawn again.
syntax:
mark flagd "reads its feature flags from Flagd"
mark config [settings] "reads its settings"
use: Use it when a node is linked from most of the diagram and those links say little more than “uses it”. The icon is the node’s own, or the one in brackets.

title: Joined links
does: Links into (or out of) a node tagged join that look the same meet a line with a dot, and one arrow reaches the node.
effect: A parallel stage reads as one: the checks close together before the gate. The label, if any, is written once. Without the tag the same is done by itself from five such links (`gather`).
syntax: ask gate [join]: all green?
use: For a parallel stage closing on a gate, or log links into one collector. Only links with the same label, style and arrowheads are joined.

title: Tables and cardinality
does: `table` nodes list columns; links to `table.column` attach at the row, with crow's feet for `[n-1]`.
effect: Every link ends at the row it is about, several links to one row are spread within it, and the ends are drawn as in an ER diagram.
use: Data models. Links name the column; `[n-1]`, `[0n-1]`, `[1-1]` give the crow's foot.

title: Sequence diagram
does: `sequence` on the first line turns the same links into messages between lifelines, top to bottom in the order written.
effect: No layout engine: participants run left to right in order of mention. Notes and `loop`, `alt`, `opt`, `par` blocks are drawn around the messages.
syntax:
sequence
client -> api : POST /jobs
api --> client : 202
use: For who says what to whom, in order. Notes and loop, alt, opt, par blocks are supported.

title: Merged links
does: Five or more links (`gather N` changes the number) to (or from) one node with the same label and style are drawn as one bus with the label once. When five or more of them come from one zone, the bus is built inside the zone (see the next entry).
effect: A trunk at the node, a line running past the sources, a short branch from each, and a dot where a branch joins. Links with different labels stay separate.
syntax: (nothing to write)
use: Automatic: five or more links (`gather N` in the diagram, `gather off` for never) to or from one node with the same label and style are merged. Give links different labels to keep them apart.

title: A junction inside a zone
does: When five or more links with the same meaning join one node to members of a zone it is not in, they meet one line inside that zone, and only one link crosses the zone’s edge.
effect: The line reaches along the members, drawn like any bus (a thin line, a dot where each link joins); each link runs straight across to it at its member’s level, and the line’s own link arrives between two of them, in the gap nearest the middle. A fan-out (a gateway into its services) has its line where the zone is entered, a fan-in (every service to an identity provider) where it is left.
syntax: (nothing to write)
use: Automatic for five or more links with the same label and style between one node and members of one zone. Links from outside that zone stay separate.

title: Folding wide strips
does: A chain that would be a strip more than four times wider than tall is folded into rows by itself.
effect: Without it the steps run in one line and the text gets small when the page is fitted to the screen. With it the chain wraps into rows. Each wrap adds one link that comes back to the start of the next row. For diagrams with frames the same idea is tried on the zones, and refused when it adds crossings or when that link would cross more than 30% of the page.
syntax: (nothing to write)
use: Automatic: a chain much wider than tall folds into rows. Write rows and columns yourself to decide where.

title: Spread links
does: Links that meet one side of a node are kept apart, and stretches of different links that would run side by side are pulled apart.
effect: Arrowheads never touch the line next to them. A short side with many links shares its room out evenly, down to about 7px apart.
syntax: (nothing to write)
use: Automatic: links are kept apart where they meet a node and where they would run side by side.
